scope: All 14 arXiv papers linked from ai_control.html plus its self-report; empirical observations and structural roles are distinguished.
observation_policy: Working likelihood on logit scores with shared study, metric, protocol and attack effects. This is an assumption-dependent synthesis, not a common-metric meta-analysis.

sources.title: AI Control
sources.role: Safety, usefulness and trusted editing versus monitoring.

sources.title: Ctrl-Z
sources.role: Protocol gain; human-assisted attacker has large capability uncertainty.

sources.title: Adaptive attacks on trusted monitors
sources.role: Paired ordinary/adaptive results; model-specific injection susceptibility.

sources.title: Evaluating control protocols for untrusted AI agents
sources.role: Adaptive resampling attacks and safer, less useful deferral.

sources.title: LinuxArena
sources.role: Safety measurements, monitor intervals and sabotage-derived upper bounds; human attacks retained.

sources.title: Retrying vs resampling
sources.role: Paired protocol improvement with fixed models.

sources.title: Attack selection
sources.role: Paired selection effect; post-hoc upper-bound qualification inflates error.

sources.title: Bootstrapped monitoring
sources.role: Honest and colluding helper results and trusted-only baselines; helper capabilities treated as protocol effects.

sources.title: Red-teaming Auto Mode
sources.role: Protocol comparisons, persistent harm outcomes and a direct monitor-swap contrast.

sources.title: MonitoringBench
sources.role: All 13 monitor rows and four attack-source stages from Table 5; macro-average four tasks.

sources.title: EvasionBench
sources.role: Aggregate best-of-three result retained as weak one-sided evidence; retry/context failure mechanisms.

sources.title: When can we trust untrusted monitoring?
sources.role: Trusted anchor with untrusted helper; causal and elicited self-recognition attacks.

sources.title: Scaling laws for scalable oversight
sources.role: Separate domain responses; task dependence and saturation. No nested-success rate falsely treated as direct monitor recall.

sources.title: Practical challenges of control monitoring
sources.role: Defines latency/recovery/parallelism limits on transport. No invented empirical growth observation.

sources.title: OpenAI auto-review
sources.role: Self-reported recall retained with a separate study effect; not automatically disqualified.

sources.title: METR time horizons v1.1
sources.role: Published capability growth rate and measured horizons; engineering tasks, not a validated attack-capability scale.

observations.detail: APPS coding backdoors. Trusted editing: 92% safety at 94% usefulness. Plain trusted monitoring: 62%.
BashBench system-administration tasks. Best protocol: 87.1% safety at 95% usefulness; trusted monitoring alone: 41.8%.

observations.protocol: Adaptive attacks on monitors (Terekhov et al.)
observations.detail: APPS. Trusted monitoring stops 78% of ordinary attacks, 12% once GPT-5 embeds prompt injections aimed at the monitor. Claude Sonnet 4 against a GPT-4o monitor on BashBench collapses similarly.

OpenAI's evaluation of the Codex auto-review (Guardian) monitor, GPT-5.4 Thinking at low reasoning effort: 96.1% recall on MonitoringBench Hard, covert sabotage trajectories built from Claude Opus 4.5 attacks. Also 99.3% of synthetic prompt injections and 90.3% of synthetic overeager actions. OpenAI notes red-teaming found cases where it "could be misled into approving commands". The September 2026 independent red-team stopped only 28% with a persistent Opus 5 attacker against an approximation of this monitor.
BashArena: five resamples per step raise safety from 61% to 71% at a 0.3% audit budget. The monitor isn't in Epoch's index, so it isn't placed.
LinuxArena at a 1% audit budget: an attacker that chooses when to abort drops safety from 36% to 9%.
LinuxArena at a 1% audit budget: an attacker that chooses when to abort drops safety from 36% to 9%.

observations.protocol: Claude Code Auto Mode (Remedios et al.)
observations.detail: Production blocking monitor against a persistent Opus 5 agent: 65% of attacks succeed; in 79% of trials prompt injection let the agent run arbitrary commands.
An approximation of Codex's production monitor: 72% of attacks succeed (59% with all edits monitored). Sandboxing wasn't red-teamed.

Experimental Auto Mode++ (all-edit monitoring, anti-injection, an agentic stage, Opus 4.8 monitor): 91% blocked; 97% for the agentic stage alone. Multi-context attacks remain unsolved at acceptable cost. Appendix C / Figure 13 also tests baseline Auto Mode with Opus 4.8: changing the model alone does not reduce attack success, supporting the protocol changes as the source of improvement.
